newsitem.title: USA: Mass. changes zero-emission vehicles regulations.
newsitem.headline: Mass. changes zero-emission vehicles regulations.

text.p: Massachusetts scaled back regulations Tuesday to force automakers to begin selling zero-emission vehicles in the state beginning in 1998, the Secretary of Environmental Affairs said.

Previously, the state required by 1998 that 2.0 percent of all vehicles sold in the state or about 6,600 cars and trucks be zero-emission vehicles by 2000 be zero-emission cars and trucks, but Massachusetts was forced to change the regulations when California scrapped its 2.0 percent plan.

The new regulations, identical to California's plan, would require the automakers to sell a total of 750 zero-emission vehicles in the state in 1998, 1,500 in 1999 and 1,500 in 2000, Secretary Trudy Coxe told Reuters.
By 2003, 10 percent of all vehicles offered for sale in the state would have to be zero-emission or electric vehicles, she said.
Under the U.S. Clean Air Act, states wishing to mandate the sale of electric vehicles must follow the California model.
"When California gave up its 2.0 percent mandate, it put the Massachusetts program at risk," she said. "We've tinkered with our rules, but we've never given up the basic premise."
Coxe said she expected the automakers to challenge the Massachusetts regulations in court, but added that since the plan is identical to California's, she believed the state is on firm legal ground.
"I suspect that they will take legal action, I don't know. That's been the way they operate," she said.
Officials with automakers were not immediately available to comment.

Mass. Governor William Weld, a long supporter of electric vehicles, unveiled in June a plan to grant tax credits to poeple who buy alternative fuel vehicles. Weld also required that 10 percent of all new vehicles pruchase by the state this year be electric, rising to 75 perent of all new vehicles by 2001.
